string.text: Many people across the Americas trace their ancestry to Akan-speaking populations due to the trans-Atlantic slave trade. Between the 17th and 19th centuries, a significant proportion of enslaved Africans shipped from the Gold Coast—estimated at 10% of all embarkations from West Africa—were of Akan origin. Although gold remained central to the Akan economy, the intensification of internal conflicts—especially among the Fante and Ashanti during the 18th century—led to the capture and external sale of war captives, many of whom were exported through coastal ports such as Anomabo and Cape Coast.

By 1715, the Algonquin peoples of the Ottawa River Valley and adjacent regions navigated a complex, transitional landscape shaped by the aftermath of the Great Peace of Montreal in 1701 and the conclusion of Queen Anne's War in 1713. Secure from the devastating, systematic Haudenosaunee (Iroquois) raids of the previous century, Algonquin bands operated within a stabilized geopolitical framework, maintaining their traditional seasonal cycles of hunting, fishing, and gathering while expanding their pivotal role as middleman traders in the French fur trade network. However, this period of relative peace brought its own pressures; the intensified focus on the fur trade altered their traditional subsistence economy, increased their reliance on European trade goods, and accelerated cultural changes as Catholic missions, such as those at Sillery and later Lake of the Two Mountains, concentrated populations and deeply influenced local social structures.

By 1715, the British colonies in North America were experiencing a period of rapid demographic growth and economic consolidation following the conclusion of Queen Anne's War. Divided into three distinct regions—the farming and maritime-focused New England colonies, the ethnically diverse agricultural Middle colonies, and the plantation-dominated Southern colonies—they were increasingly bound together by the transatlantic slave trade and mercantilist policies. While individual colonies maintained localized assemblies and distinct religious foundations, the expansion of commercial networks and a shared reliance on British manufacturing were subtly binding them to the British Empire. Concurrently, the brutal expansion of the plantation economy, particularly via the escalating importation of enslaved Africans, entrenched deep racial hierarchies that would fundamentally shape the socio-political landscape of the continent for centuries to come.

The Iroquoian peoples are an ethnolinguistic group of peoples from eastern North America. Their traditional territories, often referred to by scholars as Iroquoia, stretch from the mouth of the St. Lawrence River in the north, to modern-day North Carolina in the south. Historical Iroquoian people were the Five nations of the Iroquois or Haudenosaunee, Huron or Wendat, Petun, Neutral or Attawandaron, Erie people, Wenro, Susquehannock and the St. Lawrence Iroquoians.

Between the 9th and 15th centuries, Bantu-speaking states began to emerge in the Great Lakes region and in the savanna south of the Central African rainforests. The Monomotapa kings built the Great Zimbabwe complex, a civilisation ancestral to the Shona people. Toward the 18th and 19th centuries, the flow of Zanj slaves from Southeast Africa increased with the rise of the Sultanate of Zanzibar. With the arrival of European colonialists, the Zanzibar Sultanate came into direct trade conflict and competition with Portuguese and other Europeans along the Swahili Coast, leading eventually to the fall of the Sultanate and the end of slave trading on the Swahili Coast in the mid-20th century.

The Pirate Republic or Republic of Pirates refers to a period in the early 18th century when pirates established a self-governed, albeit informal, republic in Nassau, Bahamas. This period, during the Golden Age of Piracy, saw pirates operating with a degree of autonomy, governed by a pirate code and democratic principles within their crews.

The Sioux have two major linguistic divisions, the Dakota and Lakota peoples. Collectively, they are the Očhéthi Šakówiŋ, or 'Seven Council Fires'. The term Sioux, an exonym from a French transcription of the Ojibwe term Nadowessi, can refer to any ethnic group within the Great Sioux Nation or to any of the nation's many language dialects. Before the 17th century, the Santee Dakota lived around Lake Superior with territories in present-day northern Minnesota and Wisconsin. They gathered wild rice, hunted woodland animals, and used canoes to fish. Wars with the Ojibwe throughout the 18th century pushed the Dakota west into southern Minnesota, where the Western Dakota (Yankton, Yanktonai) and Lakota (Teton) lived.

Queen Nanny was a legendary leader of the Windward Maroons in Jamaica and a revered Jamaican National Hero. Born in West Africa and enslaved as a youth, she escaped into Jamaica's rugged Blue Mountains. There, she commanded an independent community of formerly enslaved people and led a successful guerrilla war that forced the British to recognize Maroon sovereignty in 1739

Edward Teach, best known as Blackbeard, was a notorious English pirate who terrorized the West Indies and the American colonies. Operating his famous ship, the Queen Anne's Revenge, he cultivated a terrifying, demonic persona by weaving slow-burning fuses into his hair and beard during battle. Despite his fearsome reputation, he relied more on psychological intimidation than actual violence. His brief but infamous career ended in November 1718 when he was killed in a ferocious battle by Royal Navy sailors under Lieutenant Robert Maynard.

Samuel Black Sam Bellamy (1689–1717) was a charismatic English sailor who became one of history's most successful and wealthiest pirates. Nicknamed the Prince of Pirates and the Robin Hood of the Sea for his egalitarian crew policies and mercy toward captives, he captured over 50 ships in just one year. His brief but legendary career ended when his flagship sank in a violent storm off Cape Cod.

In 1715, the Caddoan peoples lived in dense, sophisticated agricultural communities across the Piney Woods and river valleys of modern-day Texas, Louisiana, Arkansas, and Oklahoma. Organized into three primary, powerful confederacies—the Hasinai, Kadohadacho, and Natchitoches—they maintained a complex, highly stratified society governed by hereditary religious elites (xinesi) and political chiefs (caddi). They were master farmers, cultivating extensive fields of maize, beans, and squash, which sustained a vibrant regional trading network that exchanged salt and pottery for plains buffalo hides and French trade goods. By this year, the Caddo had become crucial geopolitical players on the shifting borderlands of European colonization; they selectively allied with the French out of Natchitoches for trade and firearms while strategically tolerating and diplomatic maneuvering around the newly established Spanish Catholic missions in eastern Texas, successfully leveraging their powerful warrior society, distinct ceremonial mounds, and territorial dominance to preserve their sovereignty.

But times have changed. The richest plums of the empire's cities have fallen, and they build their walls higher than they once did. The akan lords pay less for a siegemaster, and that pay is often late. So I am up to taking other employment, if it is offered.

It was time to teach them a lesson, but my brothers had a fit of cowardice. So they brokered a deal, and I was forced to leave. How do you like that?

Eventually I found an animal whose owner hadn't tied up too well as he went off to get drunk. So I took it and ran. And you know what? The cursed beast threw me, not one league out of town, and ran back to his sodden master.

They told me I had a choice: do my duty, or I would no longer be of their blood. So be it. I chose exile. Why should more men die?

Did that for 15 years, and I'm still getting less pay than some boy fresh of his mother's tit who happens to own a horse. Piss on that, I said, and I went looking for other work.

So here I am, looking to make a living through the only means I know - shedding other people's blood. Got work?

Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. Aye, real honor is as scarce as hen's teeth these days.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Oh well. I guess you've got spirit.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. A noble decision!
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Indeed. Good infantry is the backbone of an army.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. Indeed. Misfortune does not mean you must submit to humiliation.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. I guess there's something to be learned from those skilled at all trades.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. Such a cruel decree...
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Yes, I suppose you did what you had to do.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. I'm sorry for your loss. You drew a cruel lot in life.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. I'm sure he'll be happy if you're happy.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. How virtue has crumbled since the old days.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Strange thing, how people don't wish to die in someone else's quarrel.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Hah! May all thieves fail as you did.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. What? Does no one respect their parents anymore?
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Resentment is poison to an army. Men must learn to follow what orders they are given.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. As well they should have. Those who curse their protectors deserve no home.
I am of the Asante, child of the golden stool. Sounds like justice served.
From the Bono heartland I carry my father's lessons. Sensible man, that Urkhun. Nomads are the enemy of order.
I am Fante-born, and my tale begins by the sea. Necessity or not, you seem to take pride in what you did.
I am Akyem, raised in the forest, strong with spear and bow. Every day, I give thanks to the Heavens that I was not born a savage.
Among the Akuapem hills I learned my ways. You must have broken your poor father's heart.

I am from one of the lesser known clans of the athabaskan. We take the name of an undistinguished younger son of the Qildi line from five generations back. We have never held fiefs or won much wealth, but when the Qild called out their kinfolk, or the tribes were summoned by the Sultan, we took our place in the battle line.

Ah, yes - well, it would be beneath someone with a lineage like mine to pledge allegiance to the current parvenus who call themselves the emirs of the athabaskan. So, I fight for those who pay me my value in denars, good noble denars.

But I had killed three men with a spear that day, and found I had a taste for it. And I learned that thieves grow rich, while honest men die. So I lived in the hills, and took the cows of families more fortunate then my own. But I sold the cows I took, and kept the denars close to my chest.

I am from one of the lesser known clans of the caddoan. We take the name of an undistinguished younger son of the Qildi line from five generations back. We have never held fiefs or won much wealth, but when the Qild called out their kinfolk, or the tribes were summoned by the Sultan, we took our place in the battle line.

Ah, yes - well, it would be beneath someone with a lineage like mine to pledge allegiance to the current parvenus who call themselves the emirs of the caddoan. So, I fight for those who pay me my value in denars, good noble denars.
I fancy myself a healer, you see. My parents sent me to a Mercian monastery when I was young to study both prayers and herbs.
I was born in Normandy, trained as a squire for Duke Robert. When the Conqueror’s sons called for men in England, I came to serve.
I was born out of wedlock. My father raised me, but I had no inheritance. I took up the sword to make my own way.
I fought in Normandy, then England, under William and his sons. I have seen sieges and battles that younger men would not survive.
But the monasteries... lovely gardens, rich libraries, yet the dawn prayers and endless copying of texts felt hollow. I left to see the world.
I saw castles and villages, and the cost of loyalty. I fought in skirmishes, learned quickly the harsh lessons of war.
I took his sword and learned to fight. Hunger and rage were my teachers, survival my creed.
I joined my village’s levy to defend against Norman tax collectors. None wished to fight, so I volunteered, earning my first taste of battle.
Lords often send men to die for coin or land. I tire of serving such masters. My sword is mine to offer, not theirs.
I joined armies as a healer, tending to wounds both of flesh and spirit. I found I did more good on the road than among monks.
Now I roam, seeking a lord who respects skill and courage, one who rewards action rather than birth.
Soon I was no mere widow, but a warrior in my own right, feared more than pitied.
At a ford, I stayed behind while the rest fled, facing an enemy cavalry force alone. I survived, but it changed me forever.
I wander now, offering service to causes that respect honor, or to lords who value men as more than tools.
I look for campaigns where I might serve and gain experience, learning more of both herbs and men.
I offer my sword to any lord in need, hoping to earn my spurs and honor in England.
I travel, spreading news and tales. Sometimes they earn coin. Sometimes they stir hearts.
Now I wander, lending my sword to those who pay, or those who fight Normans still.
I wander now, offering my blade to lords or causes that need a man who fears neither danger nor duty.
I take work with lords who respect knights, or with men who fight for survival. That is all.
I was a monk, but ill-suited to monastery life. I learned herbs and healing, and now wander, offering my skills to armies and lords alike.
I am a Norman squire in England. Trained in arms, I wander seeking opportunity to prove myself and earn my knighthood.
I am an Anglo-Saxon minstrel, a singer of tales and bearer of news, wandering with harp and voice.
I am a Norman mercenary captain, seasoned by war, seeking service wherever coin is offered and men are needed.
I am an Anglo-Saxon widow turned warrior, forged by grief and hunger, offering my blade to causes worthy of it.
I am an Anglo-Saxon outlaw, born out of wedlock. I fight to survive and seek a new path where I can earn my place.
I am a Norman veteran knight. I fought in Normandy and England, and now wander in search of honor and purpose.
Of course - and I'm sure you'll agree it's a tale worth telling!
A squire learning the ways of war in a foreign land.
A minstrel’s song carries farther than any spear.
A veteran who knows both glory and folly.
The road from squire to knight is hard and full of tests.
You fight with verse and melody, not steel.
Skill without a cause can be wasted. You seek rightly.

I am from one of the lesser known clans of the iroquois. We take the name of an undistinguished younger son of the Qildi line from five generations back. We have never held fiefs or won much wealth, but when the Qild called out their kinfolk, or the tribes were summoned by the Sultan, we took our place in the battle line.

Ah, yes - well, it would be beneath someone with a lineage like mine to pledge allegiance to the current parvenus who call themselves the emirs of the iroquois. So, I fight for those who pay me my value in denars, good noble denars.
I am an engineer, trained in fortifications and siegecraft under the old imperial army. When the legions fell apart, many of my colleagues went into the lords' employ. I stayed true to my craft.
I have fought across Italy and beyond. My enemies have many names for me; some call me brave, others reckless. I answer only to myself.
My father was a cataphract in the east. We owned a modest estate to support his horse and armor. I was raised to follow in his path.
I am a soldier by trade. I served in the Italian legions for twenty years, until betrayal and misfortune fractured our forces.
I ran away from my village to join men who made their living on the roads. Life plowing fields seemed too harsh for me.
My family? I care little for them. I left as a child and never regretted it. My brothers can keep their inheritance.
I once followed Ladimos the Red, who preached rebellion against merchants and landowners. Many of us believed, others followed for debt or mischief.
My family owed debts, so I enlisted disguised as a man under a local commander. I preferred action to domestic life.
My father was a grain merchant in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. We lived comfortably until riots destroyed our home.
As a child, I ran with a gang called the Centaurs in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}, running errands from pickpocketing to knife work.
Nepotism runs rampant among engineers these days. Brothers and old apprentices get contracts while competent hands like mine are overlooked.
Every fight I entered, I respected the rules. If you were my enemy, I gave you your chance, but never the innocent.
But the Cumans overran our land, and he was slain. I could not take up his horse and armor, so I turned to merchants, offering my skill for hire.
Many comrades died when Drosios Neretzes led an ambush against us. I was laid up sick. The army was never the same afterward.
Bandits are brutal animals—drunken, stabbing, dying of plague or hanging. I quickly learned the risks of that life.
I fought in many wars. Comrades turn on each other in the end, and I prefer to keep my distance.
We built a backcountry temple called the Kingdom of Truth, and fought imperial detachments. When Ladimos died, our group broke apart. Some turned to extortion to survive.
Dressing as a man was simple. I bound my chest and observed the duties without difficulty.
The guards burned our neighborhood. My father tried to save his strongbox but was killed. We joined refugees, living by our wits in the countryside.
I grew older and escaped the harassment of drunken men. Unsure where to go, I sought freedom.
I refuse to cut corners. If a wall will crumble, I will say so. That honesty has kept me from the easier work, but I sleep soundly.
War is no game. Streets are no arena. If someone crosses you, act decisively. That is all one can trust in this life.
I work as a hired sword for merchants, yet I hope one day to reclaim the land I need to serve properly as my father did.
The legions fell into the hands of the wealthy, who maintained soldiers at their own expense. Squabbling factions replaced discipline, and we were mocked by former enemies.
I left that life, paid some friends to remove my name from the outlaw list, and became a law-abiding citizen, though I still enjoy the thrill of a fight.
My past is mine alone. I speak little of it.
I left, and the emperor sent troops to finish the Kingdom of Truth. Former comrades now serve lords or languish in cages marked R for robber.
An ambush led to a rout. I survived, but the army life ended for me. Glory hounds led me to near death.
I took a sword from a drunken guardsman. It has been invaluable since.
So I roam from town to town, taking work where I can find it—supervising construction, dismantling faulty defenses, or aiding in siege craft.
Merchants hire me as muscle or guard, but I owe allegiance to no one. I am a soldier of fortune, nothing more, nothing less.
I try to choose my masters wisely, hoping that some honor from my equestrian training rubs off even in the courts of commerce.
I now sell my sword to worthy commanders, training footmen and handling siege equipment for those who will follow skill over money.
Life in the city suits me better. The work can be rough, but I can relax afterward with better company than the forests offered.
I fight for a living. I will take work others shy from, and I am skilled enough to handle it.
I learned skills for survival in the hills and on caravan routes. Now I seek honest work where I can use them.
Merchants now give me work. I can wield, repair, or craft weapons and seek a captain with a company to join.
I adapt quickly. I could serve a warlord if given the chance, learning whatever skills are needed.
I am an engineer trained in the imperial army. I travel for work, supervising construction, destruction, and siegecraft wherever needed.
I am a soldier of fortune. I fight for coin, skill, and survival—not for any lord or crown.
I am a former imperial cataphract, now a mercenary for merchants, maintaining the skills and honor of my father where I can.
I am a soldier of the imperial legions, now a wandering instructor and mercenary, turning youths into disciplined fighters.
I dabbled in crime as a youth, then struck out on my own. I am honest now, though I enjoy a fight when necessary.
I kill for a living. I take the work others will not, and I do it well.
Once a rebel in the hills, I now seek honest work, skilled in survival and tracking.
I disguised myself to serve in the legions. Many have done the same, and survived to tell it.
I am a merchant's daughter displaced by riots. Survival taught me skills that now keep me wandering yet capable.
A cavalier of the Italian doing errands for traders! The shame of it!

My father learned his trade in the time of the old Urkhun Khan. Back then, the Turkics were invincible in battle, but had little knowledge of rams, catapults or even ladders, and even the most humble fortress defied them.

I rode for years behind Monchug Khan, even before he was khan. I had good name and a good sum of money. There was a girl in a neighboring village, quiet thing but good childbearing hips, who I thought would make a good bride.

I grew up in a village not far from here. My father was a peddler, and I used to go around with him, buying broken goods, repairing them, making a denar here and a denar there. But you know how the tribes from the steppe look down on those who scrape and save for the pennies to pay our taxes. Trampling our crops, hauling us off to war, sitting their in the saddle looking pleased with themeselves as we grub in the mud.

A man of another clan slew my father. My father had slain his uncle many years before. It was my job to avenge my father, but the plague carried off his killer first. So I would be expected to kill his brother instead. This is how it is with us.
I've fought for Ulus Khan, and for Monchug Khan, and even for the old Urkhun. But I fight on foot - my family's from the town, not the steppe. Life's a little different for us.

My clan was among the last of the Turkics to live out on the open steppe, moving from place to place in the old way. It was not a large clan; you would not have heard of it. It became even smaller when our encampment was surprised by an imperial patrol, and our flocks slain and scattered. Those of us who survived were forced to refuge in a village, under a larger clan, whose name you may know, but I shall not mention it.

Some boys help their fathers sew crops. Some boys learn to herd sheep. Me, I spent my childhood learning to harvest the back alleys outside winehouses. My father taught me. He was a good teacher, if a cruel man.

You probably know that the Turkics once lived out on the open grass. But our khans became used to luxuries. They lived in cities, and wished to trade with and make war upon other kings. Khan Urkhun, whom some call the Great and others call the Cruel, decided the clans must live in fixed places, so he could count their warriors and levy them, and count their flocks and tax them. Thirty years ago Khan Urkhun ordered all the clans of the Turkics to claim land and live upon it, and the noyans to build castles. Most complied, for they had come to value their comforts more than their freedom.

Slavers took me when I was a girl. The Empire tell legends of warrior-women out in the deep steppe, and when I was sold, they claimed I was one of these - to fight other slaves, to entertain them by making their legends come true.

My father died shortly after my mother became pregnant with me. I was her only child. Like most of our people, she had wanted sons. So she raised me as a son, and boasted of me like she would boast about a son. When I was a baby, she boasted of how swiftly I emptied her breast of milk. When I was a girl, she boasted of how I killed steppe ducks with my bow. When I became a woman, she boasted that soon I would be the first of my age-set to bring home the head of an enemy slain in battle.

I was the brat of a caravan guard. Never knew my mother, but my Da kept me close. I grew up running between the legs of camels on the steppe, eavesdropping on merchant gossip in the sarais, eating sesame cakes bought me by the other guards. A happier childhood you couldn't imagine.

So Urkhun, a man of vision, offered to pay the weight in silver of any imperial engineer captured alive. These captives were forced to teach men like my father the art of siegecraft. My father, in turn, taught me.

So I went to her brother, and offered him 50 sheep - a good price. But he said he wasn't giving his sister to a 'man like me.' Asked him what he meant by that, and he didn't answer, so I gave him a good punch. Maybe a couple punches - no more. Shouldn't have hurt a real man, but this little whelp died on me.

At any rate, that wasn't the life for me. So I made up my mind to run off to the grasses, find one of those tribes that doesn't answer to the khan and takes in fugitives. The Karakhuzaits, they call them. Problem is I first needed a horse.

I wanted to go to the other clan and negotiate a settlement. I had always had a talent for setting conflicts, and in this case it seemed to me clearly that fate had ended the feud. But my mother begged me not to; my cousins begged me not to. They said I should spill blood, not words.

The horse lords, the men of the great tribes - well they gallop here, and they gallup there, shooting this and shooting that. They win battles, I'll give them that. But at the end of the day, if the enemy's still laughing at you behind their walls, all that galloping means nothing.

They protected us, but they treated us with contempt. We were told to hew wood for them, to bring them water. We submitted. For the sake of our old, of our nursing mothers, we submitted. But it was hard for the young men to take.

If a man was drunk enough, I could usually take their purse without them even knowing, although sometimes they required a small knock on the head. Only travellers, though - much less fuss afterwards. Every trade takes finesse, as my father said.

Some resisted. The Karakhergit - you may have heard of them. They still dwell in the steppes but they are outcaste, raided for slaves by the others. My people were the Uvait. We were broken up - some bands were lured into the villages with silver, others were hunted down, defeated, and their sons taken as hostages.

Well, perhaps there is something to those legends, because I did very well for myself, and made my master very rich. Imperial law now decrees that men are not allowed to kill in the arena, but no one pries into what happens at the private entertainments of the rich, and over a score of my fellow slaves must have felt my blade in their chest.

Because I loved my mother, and because I was faster and stronger than the boys, I did all that she said I would do. Of those born in my year, I was the first to kill an enemy. My mother boasted even more, so that the other women came to hate her. They turned us all out of our encampment. We were forced to sell our lands and our slaves, as we could not take them with us, and we were given but a fraction of the price. All we had was our sheep. Of course raiders found us soon enough, and killed my mother, and took our flock. I escaped.

But when I got older, well, it wasn't so easy to take me on the road. Too many boys giving me funny looks. And my Da, he wanted a good husband for me, but the boys he knew weren't the marrying type. So I said to him, 'I'll be like you, Da, carry a sword and guard rich merchants. And maybe, with the money I earn, some decent boy will love me for my dowry, if not my family name.' He fussed a bit about that but he had no better ideas.

Now, in Urkhun's day, if a Turkic apprenticed in siegecraft went to work for another master, it meant a very painful death if he was recaptured. But times have changed. The richest plums of the empire's cities have fallen, and they build their walls higher than they once did. The Turkic lords pay less for a siegemaster, and that pay is often late. So I am up to taking other employment, if it is offered.

Well, you know how these things go - his kin came to our village looking for my blood. They didn't find me, but wounded one of my cousins. It was time to teach them a lesson, but my brothers had a fit of cowardice. So they brokered a deal, and I was forced to leave. How do you like that?

Anyway I hung around the marketplace in Chaikand, looking for a likely candidate. Eventually I found an animal whose owner hadn't tied up too well as he went off to get drunk. So I took it and ran. And you know what? The cursed beast threw me, not one league out of town, and ran back to his sodden master.

MY family said others would mock my father's memory. They said no one would fear to steal our sheep and horses, to molest my sisters. They told me I had a choice: do my duty, or I would no longer be of their blood. So be it. I chose exile. Why should more men die?

We foot-sloggers, we're the ones who go up the ladder and into the meat grinder. Did that for 15 years, and I'm still getting less pay than some boy fresh of his mother's tit who happens to own a horse. Piss on that, I said, and I went looking for other work.

Perhaps I was prouder than most, or quicker to anger. One day one of them insulted my lineage, and I insulted his. I was angry but my words were ill-chosen. Our protectors said they would no longer protect us if I remained among them. So, my clan banished me.

A wise man, my father. But proud, and that was his undoing. A thief cannot be proud. We do not survive long without protection from the guards, and a new captain wanted to double the 'tax' my father paid. He refused, so they hanged him.

I am one of those whose clan was hunted down a generation ago when they refused the decree of Urkhun Khan, that they must settle and be taxed. They took our flocks, and we have since lived like beggars on the edge of the towns. The far grass teases us with its beauty, but if we went there with no sheep, we would soon starve.
I feel no guilt - they were trying to kill me, and some came very close. I did what I needed to do.
I wandered a bit on the steppe. I starved a bit. But I followed the raiders and one, when he went beyond the campfire to empty his bladder, did not return. I now have his purse and his sword.

So here I am. Guess I'm not so interested in the marriage part, but I like the denars and I like my freedom. Maybe some day I'll surprise my Da with a nice farm and a couple of slaves to keep him happy in his old age.
Indeed... Well, at any rate, if you find there is an inconvenient wall between you and the object of your desire, and you wish it reduced to rubble, you know where to find me.
Let me tell you something - I'm sick of cowardice, sick of those who don't stand by their comrades and their kin.

Anyway, I guess I need a new plan to make my way in the world. But I'm not going to be a peddlar like my dad, I'll tell you that much. Maybe I'll fight and ride, or maybe I'll be a rich merchant running caravans, but one way or the other, I intend to find my place among the hawks of the world rather than the pigeons.

If an enemy chooses to stand in a battle-line and face my arrows, I would not hesitate to kill him. But our feuds - I cannot accept that I have no choice but to kill a man who had no choice but to be my enemy. I left my people. Here I can choose what I do.
At any rate, I'll fight for any man willing to take the same risks that his men face.

A man must eat. It's easy to find traders on the steppe and take their horses. But a man, unless he wishes to live like a beast, must also have people to buy those wares and give him food and blankets. There are merchants here, in the towns, who will buy horses without asking too many questions, and sometimes have other work for me.
I too am proud. So, I cannot work as a thief. Now I am looking for work that doesn't require me to bend down to the whims of guards, dogs and turnkeys.

I have scraped together a few coins. I will not say how, but they were enough to buy a sword. I am determined to earn enough to buy my people what was taken away from them - herds. I am sad to say I know little of the steppe, but I know much of the towns, of the back streets, of how to live in the gutters and shadows and grow strong.

There's not much more to say. My master was a sadistic animal but he let me keep my winnings, and eventually buy my freedom. I think he may also have realized that eventually, had he kept me against my will, he'd have ended up with a severed neck vein. So here I am, looking to make a living through the only means I know - shedding other people's blood. Got work?
I could return to my people, I suppose, but I have no wish to do so. So I am here, in the towns, where I can make good money with my sword and care nothing about those who envy me.
So like I said: I can ride, swing a sword, manage a caravan, and I have good idea how to turn a profit. You know anyone looking to hire someone like that?

My father was one of the men that Urkhun Khan had trained by captured imperial engineers. Our people knew little of siegecraft in those days. Well, he was not allowed to work for anyone but the Khan, or he would be killed in a very unpleasant way. But he taught me, his son, what he knew, and in this generation things are a little more lenient. So I can work for whom I please.

I rode behind the banner of the Turkic khan for years. I should have had a place of honor in his hall. But I killed a man from a richer clan over an insult, and he had too many kinfolk for me to linger anymore.

I was the son of a village peddler but that's not the kind of life I want to live. I want to learn to fight and ride. There are a lot of us lads like that in the Turkic lands, I think you'll find, even if the great horse lords think we're fit only to stitch sandals or push a plough.

My clan was locked in a feud with another clan for years. One life of theirs, then one life of ours, year after year, decade after decade. But I chose to break the cycle. I left my family. I am not the first to do so. This happens among us, from time to time, though few speak of it.

I was an spearman. I fought on foot. That's usually what you do if you're not from a big clan. Twice the risk, half the pay and none of the glory. Anyway, I'm done with that for now, looking for other work.

My family lost their herds and land in a dispute, and so we pledged ourself to another clan as our protectors. They treated us like servants. Once I stood up for myself, and ended up killing one of our 'protectors' in a fight. They say that is a great shame to do, but it seems that whatever happens to you, once you've tasted defeat, you encounter shame.

My father was a robber and a murderer. We preyed on drunks and travellers outside the caravanserais, mostly, only knifing them when we needed to. But the guards caught up with my father, eventually. He had enough silver stored away to pay the bribes to save one of us. He was hanged, I fled.

Urkhun Khan decreed a generation ago that all the Turkics must settle, to be conscripted and taxed. We refused. His men took our flocks, and we have since lived like beggars on the edge of the towns. I have resolved to go out and earn the money we need to buy new flocks, and then we shall go again into the great grass, beyond the reach of any tyrant or khan.

I was enslaved by imperial raiders and taken to the city. I was bought by a nobleman, who had me fight other slaves for his personal amusement. But I purchased my freedom, eventually, and now intend to enjoy it.

My father died shortly after my birth. I was my mother's only child. Our clan was poor, and a woman with a baby - especially a girl-baby - was only a drain on what little they had. So we were sold to another clan, as servants. Some years later, when my mother died, I stole one of their swords and one of their horses and rode off into the grass.

I was the child of a caravan guard. I spent my babyhood swinging from a sling on the side of a camel, and my childhood chasing strays. But caravans are preyed upon by bandits and others, and I decided I don't like being prey. I reckon I have the skills to be a predator.
My story? Certainly I can tell you, if it interests you.
You know, you'd think this place could serve proper kumis, instead of this piss they call wine... Sorry, where were we? Ah yes, my story.
Mm. Oh yes, you may.
I am from one of the highland clans, in the far east. I do not know if you are familiar with their ways. I will try to explain.
Yeah... I'll tell you a tale of life in the great Turkic hordes, terror of the world.
I'll tell you my story. But if you would judge me for what I do, you're welcome to do so, but I do not care to hear it.
Ah... Very well, I can satisfy your curiosity.
I will tell you. If you are a partisan of the Khan Urkhun and his brood, however, you may not like it.
Oh yes. I do indeed have a story to tell you.
Well, if you wish to know how cruel a pack can be to one of its own, I could enlighten you.
Sure. You can't sell a horse if you don't shout its praises, as they say.
Of course, of course. A good engineer deserves his pay.
Aye, real honor is as scarce as hen's teeth these days.
Oh well. I guess you've got spirit.
A noble decision!
Indeed. Good infantry is the backbone of an army.
Indeed. Misfortune does not mean you must submit to humiliation.
I guess there's something to be learned from those skilled at all trades.
Such a cruel decree...
Yes, I suppose you did what you had to do.
I'm sorry for your loss. You drew a cruel lot in life.
I'm sure he'll be happy if you're happy.
How virtue has crumbled since the old days.
Strange thing, how people don't wish to die in someone else's quarrel.
Hah! May all thieves fail as you did.
What? Does no one respect their parents anymore?
Resentment is poison to an army. Men must learn to follow what orders they are given.
As well they should have. Those who curse their protectors deserve no home.
Sounds like justice served.
Sensible man, that Urkhun. Nomads are the enemy of order.
Necessity or not, you seem to take pride in what you did.
Every day, I give thanks to the Heavens that I was not born a savage.
You must have broken your poor father's heart.

I am from one of the lesser known clans of the muskogean. We take the name of an undistinguished younger son of the Qildi line from five generations back. We have never held fiefs or won much wealth, but when the Qild called out their kinfolk, or the tribes were summoned by the Sultan, we took our place in the battle line.

Ah, yes - well, it would be beneath someone with a lineage like mine to pledge allegiance to the current parvenus who call themselves the emirs of the muskogean. So, I fight for those who pay me my value in denars, good noble denars.
I fancy myself a healer, you see. My parents sent me to a Mercian monastery when I was young to study both prayers and herbs.
I was born in Normandy, trained as a squire for Duke Robert. When the Conqueror’s sons called for men in England, I came to serve.
I was born out of wedlock. My father raised me, but I had no inheritance. I took up the sword to make my own way.
I fought in Normandy, then England, under William and his sons. I have seen sieges and battles that younger men would not survive.
But the monasteries... lovely gardens, rich libraries, yet the dawn prayers and endless copying of texts felt hollow. I left to see the world.
I saw castles and villages, and the cost of loyalty. I fought in skirmishes, learned quickly the harsh lessons of war.
I took his sword and learned to fight. Hunger and rage were my teachers, survival my creed.
I joined my village’s levy to defend against Norman tax collectors. None wished to fight, so I volunteered, earning my first taste of battle.
Lords often send men to die for coin or land. I tire of serving such masters. My sword is mine to offer, not theirs.
I joined armies as a healer, tending to wounds both of flesh and spirit. I found I did more good on the road than among monks.
Now I roam, seeking a lord who respects skill and courage, one who rewards action rather than birth.
Soon I was no mere widow, but a warrior in my own right, feared more than pitied.
At a ford, I stayed behind while the rest fled, facing an enemy cavalry force alone. I survived, but it changed me forever.
I wander now, offering service to causes that respect honor, or to lords who value men as more than tools.
I look for campaigns where I might serve and gain experience, learning more of both herbs and men.
I offer my sword to any lord in need, hoping to earn my spurs and honor in England.
I travel, spreading news and tales. Sometimes they earn coin. Sometimes they stir hearts.
Now I wander, lending my sword to those who pay, or those who fight Normans still.
I wander now, offering my blade to lords or causes that need a man who fears neither danger nor duty.
I take work with lords who respect knights, or with men who fight for survival. That is all.
I was a monk, but ill-suited to monastery life. I learned herbs and healing, and now wander, offering my skills to armies and lords alike.
I am a Norman squire in England. Trained in arms, I wander seeking opportunity to prove myself and earn my knighthood.
I am an Anglo-Saxon minstrel, a singer of tales and bearer of news, wandering with harp and voice.
I am a Norman mercenary captain, seasoned by war, seeking service wherever coin is offered and men are needed.
I am an Anglo-Saxon widow turned warrior, forged by grief and hunger, offering my blade to causes worthy of it.
I am an Anglo-Saxon outlaw, born out of wedlock. I fight to survive and seek a new path where I can earn my place.
I am a Norman veteran knight. I fought in Normandy and England, and now wander in search of honor and purpose.
Of course - and I'm sure you'll agree it's a tale worth telling!
A squire learning the ways of war in a foreign land.
A minstrel’s song carries farther than any spear.
A veteran who knows both glory and folly.
The road from squire to knight is hard and full of tests.
You fight with verse and melody, not steel.
Skill without a cause can be wasted. You seek rightly.

I'm an engineer. Most of us learned our trade and got our contacts through the army. It was a good system: it was the emperor's money, so the emperor's servants kept a close eye on us. But as everyone knows, the emperor ran out of money. The lords are in charge of fortifications now, and all they have to go on is the say-so of other engineers.
See, there's a lot of tales about me, and only some of them are true. The Turks call me by one name, the Arabs by another.

I'm a surgeon. I trained at the imperial academy in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. I had many rich and influential patients in the town. I thought I was well shielded from the intrigues and dangers of the Portuguese.

My father was an imperial cataphract. Alas, he died in battle against the Arabs, and I was placed under the local archon's guardianship. He had eyes for my father's estate, modest as it was, so he arranged for me to be married to his cousin.
My father was a cataphract in the east. We had a small estate to pay for his horse and armor. I was raised to take his place on the imperial troop rosters when he came of age.

I'm a soldier by trade. I've served in the portugueses' legions for 20 years. Once upon a time they were worthy of being called 'legions.' We served together for years, and we'd die rather than see our standards falter or fall.

Me and some lads from my village, we thought we'd run away, join some other lads up there who make their living on the highways, if you know what I mean. Didn't much want to go scratching a plow across the dry fields all year every year like my father did.
What do you want to know about? My family? Piss on them. I left home as a child and never had cause to regret it. My brothers can take my inheritance, and I hope they choke on it.

You may have heard of Ladimos the Red. He preached that the Heavens were getting ready to unload their wrath on landowners and merchant, that we had to drive them out and live pure lives and we'd be rewarded with a Pure Emperor, come down from the skies. This was some 10 years ago. Well, a lot of us ran off to follow him, some of us believed him and some of us had debts and some just wanted to take a lick at those that oppressed us.

My family had debts, so I signed up to be a soldier under one of Old Neretzes's kinsmen. I guess I always liked men's work more than women's work. The legions took hill women as scouts but I was never the hidey-sneaky type. So I did what I did to be in the spear line.

My father was a merchant in {IMPERIALCAPITAL}. We lived in a rich house, with many servants. I wanted for nothing. Our neighbor was a moneylender, who specialized in loans to the imperial guard. That turned out to be a bad neighborhood in which to live, when the riots came.

Far back as I remember, I was living on the streets of {IMPERIALCAPITAL} with a bunch of other dirty, barefoot scrogs. A group of men in our alley, they called themselves the Centaurs, I guess they took a liking to me. Gave me special errands to run from them - started with picking pockets, ended with sticking knives into their enemies. Back then I'd do anything for a handful of figs and cheese and a pat on the head.

You can imagine - it's a bit of a racket. People build arches that fall down, and his colleagues go on recommending him because he's someone's brother or old apprentice. The greatest sin in our brotherhood is criticizing the work of other engineers.
I've been in a lot of fights and I've killed a lot of people. Ask you around - you shouldn't just take my word for it. But never one who didn't deserve it, and never once outside a fair fight.

But one day I was contacted by an agent of the Bureau of Barbarian Affairs. I do not know how well you know them. Their original mission was to keep the foreign tribes divided and weak, but they expanded their remit into all the affairs of the Portuguese, anything that might be deemed a threat. At first they wanted small harmless details about my patients. To do so was a violation of my oath, but I was anxious to have the favor of the Bureau. But soon they began to call on me for more and more.

But the Turks overran us, and he was slain, and our land was taken. Its revenues now belong to some tarkhan. Alas, the Portuguese have little land to grant today, even to trained cavalrymen like myself who wish to serve. And horses are expensive.

But the Emperor led the pick of the legions into an ambush in the German woods. You may have heard that story. I was laid up sick at the time. But a lot of my comrades didn't come back, and things were never the same afterward.

But I was young and foolish. Bandits - well, who'd have thought? They're real animals. Always drunk and stabbing each other, or too drunk to feel cold so they catch the plague and end up coughing up blood, or drunk and asleep when the patrol comes around so they end up on the gallows - I suspect you get the idea.
I've fought in a few wars, for one side or the other. You want to know about my-comrades-in-arms? Piss on them too. They all turn on you in the end.

We built a great temple in the back country, out in the bush, called it the Kingdom of Truth. We whipped two imperial detachments sent to track us down. But Ladimos died, 'Called up to Heaven' he said on his deathbed, and then we lost our way a bit. We needed food and we needed money, so our chiefs started collecting 'taxes' from the villages below. Some started taking money from lords and merchants for protection of caravans. And those who grumbled - well, they started turning up dead in the dry streambeds.
Dressed as a man, of course. Weren't difficult to do. Not hard to fool men. Bound my breasts and watched where I pissed. It was easy.

The guardsmen came to burn our neighbor's house, so their debts would be forgotten. The flames spread to our house, and it was destroyed. My father tried to save his strongbox, and that was his undoing. A riot is a holiday for thieves and robbers, and some saw him dragging it through the streets, so they knifed him and took it. We tried to find shelter with my uncle, but there was no food in the city, and he turned us out. So we joined the refugees in the country, living on what we could steal from the fields.

Got a bit older though, and their interest in me changed. Filthy drunken louts pressing themselves against me, grabbing at me - I wasn't having that. Made up my mind to leave, but wasn't sure where to go.
Well, I don't play that game. If something's going to fall down and kill someone, I'll point that out. So, naturally, all my 'brothers' cut me out of contracts.

Let me tell you something else - war is not a game. It's not a game. Play by the rules and you die. The streets aren't the arena. If you think someone's your enemy, you take them down - don't wait for a polite challenge.

You may call it pride, but I do not wish to enlist as a foot soldier. So I work here in town, for merchants, for pay, a hired sword. All I can say is that I hope one day to purchase the land I need to serve our emperor, whoever sits in the throne, as my father did.

After Arenicos's so-called reforms, they try to maintain an army on the cheap, letting the rich run the show out of their own pocket. No wonder the whole thing's collapsed into a bunch of squabbling factions and we're mocked by the barbarians we used to rule.
So that was no kind of life, neither. I left the woods, paid a little money to friends who got my name off the outlaw list, and now I'm a regular law-abiding citizen. Officially, that is.
About my past, that's all I have to say.

So I left. And a short while later the emperor sent a third detachment, bigger than the others, and that was the end of the Kingdom of Truth. My old comrades - I see them sometimes from time to time, some in a lord's retinue, others in a cage with R for 'robber' branded on their forehead.

Then one day our commander led us into an ambush. The apple doesn't far fall from the tree, you could say. I didn't see the battle but was part of the rout. That was the end of army life for me. Don't care for glory-hounding lords leading me to my death. But I still like to fight.

I found a guardsman, alone and drunk. I have no idea whether he was one of the ones that set fire to our neighborhood. Maybe I should not have done to him what I did to him. But now I have his sword. It's been very useful.

So, anyway, I am forced to spend my time in taverns, taking whatever work can be found. I can oversee the building of most structures, or, if the need is there, I am also adept at knocking them down with catapults, rams, and mines.

I don't like to brag about my own deeds, so I'll leave it at that. I do a lot of work for the merchants around here, but they don't own me. I'm my own man. I just take their money. It's not like I'm a mercenary or something like that.
I try at least to pick and choose my master, and hope at least that some of our equestrian honor rubs off on the men of commerce.

Well, I can't just sit around and drink myself to death, so I sell my sword to anyone worth following. I'm a good trainer - I don't bother with horsemen or archers, but if you've got good steady footmen I can do a lot with them. I know a bit about siege machinery too.
Life's better here in the city. More 'civilized,' you could say. Oh, the work can be a bit rough and tumble, but I feel I can relax after a long day with more refined company, like your good self.
I can fight. And I don't mind doing work that others would shirk.

I learned a few skills up in the hills, how to follow a trail and spot an ambush, most useful to caravaneers. So I reckon I can probably stay ahead of the hangman. A regular job wouldn't hurt, though.

Yeah.. The merchants give me jobs. But I'm not sure I care much for guarding caravans. A lot of sitting around listening to boring talk about prices. Look, I can wield a sword or spear and I can also repair them. Wouldn't mind trying my hand them at making them too. If you've know a captain with a good company, a fighting company, maybe he'd be interested.
I think my story shows that I am adaptable, at least. If there was room for me in a warlord's retinue, say, I imagine I could quickly learn whatever skills were needed.
I'm an engineer, with imperial army training. I'm sure by now you've met a few of us around, and know a bit about what we can do.
I'm a warrior. A soldier of fortune, you might say. A damn good one, too, as my enemies would tell you if they could speak from the other world.
I'm a former imperial cataphract. Our skills, and our honor, needs no further introduction. But I was unable to afford my horse and armor, so I took work with merchants, as a hired sword.

I'm a soldier of the imperial legions. How we came to this sorry state is a sad tale that you've no doubt heard already from my comrades. But I'm sure you're familiar with our mettle in battle, and our skill at turning youths into soldiers.

When I was a lad, I dabbled in crime and banditry a bit, but am now seeking more honest work. I still like the fighting and killing part, though. Anyway, I'm sure you've met a fair amount of men like me on your journeys.
I kill for a living. You don't look too wet behind the ears, so I'm sure I don't need to tell you any more about myself than that.
Aye, well, once I was a rebel up in the back country, but rebels never last too long. Now I just want to serve and get paid. You've been around. You've met men like me before, I'm sure.
I dressed as a man to serve in the legions. There are many of us who've done that, believe it or not. You've probably met one of us before, even if you didn't know it.

I was a merchant's daughter. There was a bout of unrest in our home city, and our home and warehouses were burned and our family made penniless. I shall spare you the details. I am sure you've heard plenty of similar tales in these times.
A cavalier of the Portuguese doing errands for traders! The shame of it!

I am Scottish. But for 20 years, I fought for the Empire. Indeed, most Scottish my age learned their trade in the legions. We saw no dishonor in it. They fed us well, they paid us well, they respected our courage.

My family was not one of the greatest clans of the Scottish, but neither are we among the poorest. When I came of age, my family sent me to join the Wolfskins. You may have heard of this tradition - for three years we live in the woods and do not eat cooked meat, wear spun cloth, or sleep under a roof, and according to the law we are beasts, not bound by the laws of men.

My uncle - he had a great herd of cows, and in the Scottish upcountry that is only kind of wealth we value. But they were taken by his chief herdsman, a man we trusted. So we took up spears to get them back, but my uncle was now poor, but the thief had many kinsmen. Having nothing else to lose, my uncle ordered that even the women of our family take up spears and ride out to fight, and so we did.

I do things in the old way, and so whenever an enemy falls to my spear, I take their head! Let's see - I have Brechtan the Old, Lamaich the Lame -- don't let the names fool you, these were great warriors - Archan the Bull, so many others! A true Scottish never boasts, because his deeds are hung over the hearth for all to see. At least that's the way it used to be.

But there's no legions any more. And since Caladog became king, well, he's gotten the young to think that to fight for the Empire is treason. Treason to what? 'scottish'? There is no scottish. Never has been. Just a bunch of quarreling warlords, who'll steal your cows as soon as you turn your back on them.

But I had killed three men with a spear that day, and found I had a taste for it. And I learned that thieves grow rich, while honest men die. So I lived in the hills, and took the cows of families more fortunate then my own. But I sold the cows I took, and kept the denars close to my chest.

Well now, I am a warrior of the Scottish. There is no greater boast than that, I will tell you! But perhaps if you hire me, I can tell you more later about the great names I have slain and the heads I have taken.

I am Scottish by birth but I served with the Empire. Many of us did. A brave lord, a captain who cares for his men... What does it matter in which language your oath of fealty is given, as long as you honor it?

I am from one of the lesser known clans of the siouan. We take the name of an undistinguished younger son of the Qildi line from five generations back. We have never held fiefs or won much wealth, but when the Qild called out their kinfolk, or the tribes were summoned by the Sultan, we took our place in the battle line.

Ah, yes - well, it would be beneath someone with a lineage like mine to pledge allegiance to the current parvenus who call themselves the emirs of the siouan. So, I fight for those who pay me my value in denars, good noble denars.

I lived in a small coastal village across the gulf. The north is a hard place — jarls quarrel over grazing and ships, and a lord’s feud can burn a whole hamlet down. My mother tended the sick with herbs and song; I learned at her knee until the raid that took her and the man I was to wed.

I was the finest youth in my village for sword and axe; folk said I fought like a berserker. At coming-of-age I rode south to find war and coin, first serving with the Vaegir guard but chafing at their discipline.

My father was a noted raider whose leg was cut in a raid and who kept us fed with spoils. We invested his victories in land and thralls, but I swore to earn for my own house and to buy a ship of my own.
I served in the imperial guard in the days of Arenicos. We were proud of order and formation, but when the emperor fell the city turned and the guard became the target of the mob.
I was a tiller of earth until a quarrel over a boundary fence ended with a man’s skull split by my hoe. Blood enmeshes a man — what started as anger took me beyond repair.

In our law when a matter cannot be settled, we let champions answer in single combat — it is an old way. If a man will not fight, he hires a champion to fight for him; the thing is that courage has a price.
My parents died when I was young and my sister married to a man who coveted the farm. He hired a crafty law-man to press his claim, and the thing awarded them our land.
My father was a draftsman, a builder for local jarls — towers, keeps and palisades. He taught me to draw plans and to mark timber for the keel and wall.
I come from a good house and always wished to be a shield-maiden. I trained with the village boys and learned the spear, but my father insisted a daughter should spin and bring dowry, not blood.
I do a man's work better than most men. I am not given to excuses: I show up sober, do the task, and collect my pay. That is my promise.

They wanted cattle and timber; they took everything else too. We fled into the birchwoods and I swore never to be helpless while others decided my fate. I will mend the wounded on the field, and if need be, I will learn to wound as well as I heal.

I then joined a shield-clan — the Skolderbroda — but their insistence on tight ranks and shield-walls bored me. I favor the bloody melee: charge, cleave, and send a man home with no use for his bragging.
I will not sell the homestead to fit out a crew, so I hire myself as a warrior until I can buy a longship and hire men to row her. I plan raids to bring back silver and people to trade or sell.
We tried to hold the peace, but loot and anger spread like wildfire. Some of my comrades looted and killed in the fury; later I would see what men do when law decays and I could not unsee it.
His kin came for blood-payment. I could have paid for one life, but not three. In the fury I killed again and then fled, for our thing would have hanged me.

I made a trade of it — championing men for coin. I fought for heads, ransoms and honor-claims. It paid well till the councils said I sold my sword too cheaply and banned me from being a lawful champion.
I left for the woods, living by trapping and selling furs. The life is quiet and it suits me better than court talk and oaths.
When he died I stayed with my uncle but the folk muttered I brought evil — a blemish on my shoulder looked like a witch-mark. The village elders demanded I leave and do not return.
I was married off and my husband insulted me in the market. I struck him down in a lawful duel, was judged not guilty by the thing — but I was disinherited and shamed, so I left.
You will not find me passed out when needed. You will not have to bribe guards to get me out of a cell. I do what must be done, and I do it well.

Perhaps one day my kin will find peace. For now I travel from longhouse to longship offering salves, poultices and steady hands to men who bleed for silver, and I will not return to be at any man's mercy again.
The captains told me to keep my mouth shut or leave; I left. Now I look for a warband that pays for a man who makes trouble and survives it.
When I have a vessel, I will sail to rich coasts and come home with enough to secure marriages for my siblings and land for my sons. Till then my sword and shield will do.
I left with nothing but the clothes on my back and one old sword. Now I roam, looking for honest pay to earn back what I lost and a captain whose men keep discipline even in hard times.
I do not boast of it. A farmer has no love for a sword, but the Heavens decided a different path. Now men in the cities pay me for sharp work that the law will not let them do.
So now I wander and mercenary-work keeps my hand. Duels are clean and quick; I prefer them to long sieges and dull guard duty. If your leader needs a man who does not flinch, my price is fair.
Now I trap and guide hunters, but I also serve as scout for war-parties that need men who can vanish into the trees and report on an enemy’s tracks.

I wandered and learned to survive among thieves and sellswords, until I stole a sword from a careless bandit and found I could trade woodcraft as well as a blade. Now I hire out as builder and muscle both.
A warrior’s life is harder than the stories; yet it is honest. I now fight for pay, free of the obligations that once bound me.
If a chief needs someone who protects his wagons or cuts down his enemies cleanly, I am that woman — and I do not ask for pity.
If you know of a warband seeking someone to bind wounds and keep men whole after a raid, send them to me.
Still, if your company wants a fighter who charges where most hesitate, I'm available for the right share.
If you know a captain who values seamanship and daring, send word — I'll earn my share and more.

I am welsh. But for 20 years, I fought for the Empire. Indeed, most welsh my age learned their trade in the legions. We saw no dishonor in it. They fed us well, they paid us well, they respected our courage.

My family was not one of the greatest clans of the welsh, but neither are we among the poorest. When I came of age, my family sent me to join the Routiers. You may have heard of this tradition - for three years we live in the woods and do not eat cooked meat, wear spun cloth, or sleep under a roof, and according to the law we are beasts, not bound by the laws of men.

My uncle - he had a great herd of cows, and in the welsh upcountry that is only kind of wealth we value. But they were taken by his chief herdsman, a man we trusted. So we took up spears to get them back, but my uncle was now poor, but the thief had many kinsmen. Having nothing else to lose, my uncle ordered that even the women of our family take up spears and ride out to fight, and so we did.

I do things in the old way, and so whenever an enemy falls to my spear, I take their head! Let's see - I have Brechtan the Old, Lamaich the Lame -- don't let the names fool you, these were great warriors - Archan the Bull, so many others! A true welsh never boasts, because his deeds are hung over the hearth for all to see. At least that's the way it used to be.

But there's no legions any more. And since that new guy became king, well, he's gotten the young to think that to fight for the Empire is treason. Treason to what? 'welsh'? There is no welsh. Never has been. Just a bunch of quarreling warlords, who'll steal your cows as soon as you turn your back on them.
Some speak well of their time in the Routiers. It is intended to teach you the ways of the woods. But the 'pack' I joined were all rich feral children, playing at being animals.

But I had killed three men with a spear that day, and found I had a taste for it. And I learned that thieves grow rich, while honest men die. So I lived in the hills, and took the cows of families more fortunate then my own. But I sold the cows I took, and kept the denars close to my chest.

I am the prince of horsethieves! I have stolen Arabs mares from amid the tents and ridden them across the desert under the moon, I have taken French stallions from their paddocks, the sturdy ponies of the Turks, and the steady geldings of the imperial lancers. But, I'll be the first to admit, it is risky work, so sometimes I do other jobs.

Well now, I am a warrior of the welsh. There is no greater boast than that, I will tell you! But perhaps if you hire me, I can tell you more later about the great names I have slain and the heads I have taken.

I am welsh by birth but I served with the Empire. Many of us did. A brave lord, a captain who cares for his men... What does it matter in which language your oath of fealty is given, as long as you honor it?
